#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)

## ARIMA vs. ETS

### 2.1 The Data

```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
```

```{r}
liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "U.S. Beer, Wine, and Liquor Store Sales",
       x = "Month", y = "Millions of dollars")

liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Plot: Log Liquor Store Sales",
       x = "Month", y = "log(sales)")
```

Sales trend steadily upward, from about \$1.4 billion in 1992 to over \$6 billion by 2019. December is the highest month by far (about 39% above an average month); January and February are the lowest (about 17% below). Summer months are somewhat above average. The seasonal swings grow with the level (the December-January gap went from about \$940M in 1992 to \$2,370M in 2019) so logs make the swings roughly constant and the seasonality additive.

### 2.2 Fit Both Models

```{r}
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

ARIMA chosen: ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)\[12\] w/ drift. No regular difference (d = 0) and one seasonal difference (D = 1): the model uses the change from the same month last year. ETS(A,A,A). Additive errors, an additive trend, and additive seasonality on log scale.

```{r}
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

arima_dof <- liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  tidy() |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "^s?(ar|ma)")) |>
  nrow()
arima_dof

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = arima_dof)
```

dof = 6. Ljung-Box statistic = 120, p-value \< 0.001, so the residuals do not look like white noise, so some structure is left.

### 2.3 The Horse Race

The TS-CV fits were run in the R script and saved to `results/`.

216 forecast origins. First forecast: January 2002. Last forecast: December 2019.

```{r}
liquor_acc <- readRDS("results/liquor_acc.rds")
liquor_acc |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

ARIMA forecasts most accurately. Both metrics agree.

### 2.4 Are the Differences Significant?

```{r}
dm_liquor <- readRDS("results/dm_liquor.rds")
dm_liquor$arima_ets
dm_liquor$arima_snaive
```

ARIMA vs ETS: DM = -2.91, p = 0.004. ARIMA vs SNAIVE: DM = -10.76, p \< 0.001. ARIMA is significantly more accurate than both ETS and the seasonal random walk. I would use ARIMA.

## Forecast Combination

### 3a

```{r}
combo_acc <- readRDS("results/combo_acc.rds")
combo_acc |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

Combo RMSE = 85.19, MAE = 66.77. It beats ETS (94.35) but not ARIMA (81.43).

### 3b

```{r}
#| eval: false
err_cor <- cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
err_cor
```

The correlation is 0.88 so the two models do make similar errors and averaging cancels a little. The DM test also showed ARIMA is significantly better than ETS, so adding ETS mostly pulls the forecast toward a worse model. Thats why the combo didn't beat ARIMA.

## VAR vs. BVAR

### 4.1 The Data

```{r}
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))

growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
nrow(y)
head(y)

N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
```

120 forecasts per variable, from 1990 Q1 to 2019 Q4.

### 4.2 OLS VARs

```{r}
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")
var_results |> select(Variable, `VAR(1)`, `VAR(4)`) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The VAR(1) forecasts better for 7 out of 8 vars (all except inflation, where the almos tie). The VAR(4) estimates many more coefficients from limited data. The extra estimation noise can outweigh what the extra lags add.

### 4.3 A BVAR

The BVAR forecasts were run in the R script and saved to `results/`.

```{r}
var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

-   BVAR(4) with lambda = 0.3 has a lower RMSE than the OLS VAR(4) for all 8 variables. The only difference is the prior: shrinking coefficients toward zero cuts estimation noise.
-   Compared with the VAR(1), the BVAR(4) is better for 3 of 8 variables, inv, infl, gs10.
-   With lambda = 0.05, RMSE rises for 7 of 8, so its too much shrinkage.
-   No. The winner's RMSE is too optimistic: the model was chosen because it did best on this same sample, partly by luck.

### 4.3c Diebold-Mariano Tests

```{r}
dm_var <- readRDS("results/dm_var.rds")
dm_var$gdp
dm_var$infl
```

GDP: DM = 2.14, p = 0.035. The BVAR is significantly more accurate. Inflation: DM = 1.45, p = 0.149. The difference is not significant. So some of the RMSE differences in 4.3b are probably just noise.

## Factor Model

### 5.1 The Data

```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,
         "2" = d(x),
         "3" = d(d(x)),
         "4" = log(x),
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]
dim(fm)

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```

-   INDPRO (5): monthly growth rate.
-   PAYEMS (5): monthly growth rate.
-   CPIAUCSL (6): change in the monthly inflation rate.
-   FEDFUNDS (2): first difference.

INDPRO is an index that grows over time, so growth rates make sense. FEDFUNDS is already a percent rate, so a simple difference is enough.

### 5.2 Estimate the Factors

```{r}
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))
summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```

The first three factors explain 29.4% of the variation (15.0%, 7.4%, and 7.1%).

```{r}
F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

Factor 1 is most correlated with employment and industrial production (PAYEMS, IPMANSICS, USGOOD, INDPRO, MANEMP) and drops in recessions, so it is a real activity factor. Factor 2 is most correlated with consumer price series (CPI and PCE price indexes), so it is a price/inflation factor.

### 5.3 Replicate the Horse Race from Class

```{r}
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}
c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```

RMSE_AR = 0.617 and RMSE_FA = 0.589, matching the results from class. the full sample factors use future data that a forecaster wouldnt normally have at the forecast, which makes the forecasts look better than they really are, sore youre forcasting information you already have.

### 5.4 A Direct Forecast of Inflation

```{r}
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)
  g <- lv$g
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

cpi_race <- direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
cpi_race |> mutate(pct_reduction = 100 * (1 - RMSE_FA / RMSE_AR))
```

Yes. RMSE falls from 2.108 to 1.894, a 10.2% reduction (MAE: 1.578 to 1.349). DM p-value = 0.0004, so difference is statistically significant.

## Reflection

I believe the biggest takeaway was that the simple models were hard to beat when the data was limited, relative to the number of parameters, the VAR(1) beat the VAR(4), and even the BVAR only beat the VAR(1) for 3 of 8 variables. The same idea came up more than once as forecasts improve when you reduce estimation noise. With shrinkage we can only do it by pulling coefficients toward zero, equal weights can also do it by not estimating combination weights at all, and factors do it by summarizing 121 series with just three. But each of those can also derail, like the BVAR with lambda = 0.05, or help little, like the combo when the errors were highly correlated. I will remark it was good practice that a little RMSE alone isn't enough, since the DM tests showed some differences were not significant.
